title: How the fleeting beauty of roses became continuous. A commentary on ‘Molecular investigation of the progenitors, origin, and domestication patterns of diploid Chinese old garden roses’
content: Plant domestication often involves human-induced hybridization between wild species. Today’s modern hybrid roses exist in tens of thousands of varieties and represent the commercially most important ornamental plants worldwide. Independently, people have been domesticating wild rose species in both Europe and Western Asia (i.e. European old garden roses), and in China (i.e. Chinese old garden roses) for over a thousand years. This long history of rose cultivation highlights how deeply plant breeding is embedded in human culture, primarily for aesthetic purposes (Altman et al., 2022). The merger between European and Chinese old garden roses (Fig. 1) in the 19th century, which was initiated by the introduction of the first modern rose cultivar, ‘La France’, in 1867, paved the way for the rapid development of these highly successful ornamentals. Deciphering the genetic origins of today’s cultivars with such ancient roots is an important step towards developing and preserving our genetic resources. Zhang et al. (2025) made a major contribution to the Chinese side of the story. This becomes all the more important given that genomic analyses of hybrid rose varieties revealed that modern roses have lost more than a quarter of their genetic diversity in less than ten generations since the creation of ‘La France’, and are far more influenced by the ancient Chinese background than by their European ancestors (Leroy et al., 2025). This is because Chinese old garden roses introduced a set of desirable traits such as the crimson or yellow petal colour, the striking fragrance reminiscent of black tea, the highly centred flower structure, and above all their ability for recurrent flowering changing the fleeting beauty of garden roses so that they become continuous. Earlier, partly genomic, studies identified two wild species (i.e. R. chinensis Jacq. and R. gigantea Crép., both section Chinenses (DC.). Ser.) as progenitors from which the Chinese old garden roses originated. Further contributions have concerned only sections of the genus and the detailed history of their origin has not yet been clarified (Tan et al., 2017; Hibrand Saint-Oyant et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2025). Excessive breeding leading to a massive production of thousands of rose varieties involving hybridization steps, selection, selfing and back-crossing naturally blurred the genetic boundaries and complicated the identification of extant wild species contributing to these ornamentals. Zhang et al. (2025) analysed 25 diploid accessions of Chinese old garden roses and their wild putative relatives to investigate their historic formation, combining information from nuclear and plastid barcoding markers, expressed sequence tag-simple sequence repeats and morphometrics. They were able to pinpoint the beginning of the story to an ancient cultivar: the diploid R. chinensis cultivated in Ya’an, Sichuan, China, which clearly showed traces of domestication such as recurrent flowering and petal numbers higher than five. However, the cultivar was closely related to wild accessions of R. chinensis and, remarkably, did not show any signs of hybridization. Starting from this ‘bridging ancient cultivar’, Zhang et al. (2025) present for the first time a stepwise scheme of hybridizations leading to four distinct groups within Chinese old garden roses (Fig. 1): the hybridization of a rose such as R. chinensis from Ya’an, Sichuan, with R. multiflora var. cathayensis Rehder & E.H. Wilson of section Synstylae DC., which introduced the trait of many-flowered corymbose inflorescences into the gene pool, resulted in the most ancient hybrid group of Chinese old garden roses, named ‘Old Blush’ (Tan et al., 2017). ‘Old Blush’ roses were then subsequently hybridized on one hand with the R. kwangtungensis T.T. Yu & H.T. Tsai species complex, a taxon endemic to south-eastern China, forming the ‘Slater’s Crimson’ group. On the other hand, ‘Old Blush’ cultivars were merged with R. gigantea, which is more widespread in South-East Asia, giving rise to the R. odorata ‘Tea Rose’ group. Moreover, ‘Old Blush’ plants were also involved in a group of more complex hybrids (e.g. ‘Clothilde Soupert’ or R. hybrida ‘Mutabilis’), to which several species of section Synstylae from China or Japan contributed. All these ancient hybrids and R. chinensis from Ya’an, Sichuan, exhibit the highly desirable trait of recurrent flowering explained by a mutation of the floral repressor gene, RoKSN. So far, several mutated alleles of this gene located on chromosome 3 are known (Iwata et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2017; Hibrand Saint-Oyant et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2025). In modern roses several independent insertions of the copia retrotransposon within the RoKSN gene have been documented (Iwata et al., 2012; Soufflet-Freslon et al., 2021), but also another allele, RoKSNNULL, with a large inversion was detected in the progeny of the previously sequenced genome of an ‘Old Blush’ accession. Thus, the trait of recurrent flowering has been obviously introduced or modified via different pathways in modern roses, but the history of its transmission is still not understood.
